tier_reason: First-party league log (tests/aac_league_v0.8.txt) produced by the project's own public harness tests/compare_encoders.py, with ffmpeg native AAC in every table; no compiler, flags or CPU model in the log (the README prose names only 'an M1'), so it cannot reach A and is not independent.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: README build instructions use CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; the compiler and the flags used for the league run are not stated
corrections.caveats: Very new project (first commits July 2026, 322 commits, 2 stars) with first-party measurements only; compiler and flags not stated, CPU only named as M1 in README prose (the league includes afconvert, so it ran on macOS). The harness (tests/compare_encoders.py) times one subprocess.run per encoder and clip with time.time(), so each 'enc x' figure is a single wall-clock run that includes process start-up, WAV parsing and file output; ffmpeg's heavier start-up weighs more on short clips, and clip lengths are not published (the clips are local files). The README's '~272x/168x realtime at -q speed/-q best' does not match the v0.8 log, where glint-best ranges 164x-283x (mean about 228x, derived from page data), so the prose figure comes from another run. Quality is not traded for the win over ffmpeg: glint -q normal beats ffmpeg-aac on mean NMR on all 6 clips at 128 kbps, but trails Apple and FDK on speech and electronic. vo-aacenc is about as fast as glint -q normal on some rows (castanets 256 kbps 260x vs 241x) at much worse quality. MP3 comparison against LAME is quality-first, not speed.

notes: Every quoted ffmpeg-aac vs glint-normal row matches the log, and the 2.1x-9.8x range checks out across all 12 rows (lowest industrial 128 kbps 175/84, highest electronic 256 kbps 246/25). Speed is wall-clock of whole CLI runs, single sample, so treat the ratios as indicative. Metadata (MIT, 2 stars, last commit 2026-08-19, not a fork) confirmed.

tier_reason: First-party README table; LibFResample side timed by its own tests/benchmark.py, libsamplerate side taken from SRC's own throughput test divided by 44100, compilers named but no flags and CPUs given only as clock and family (e.g. '3.2 GHz AMD Phenom II'), so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Stereo, System C (3.2 GHz AMD Phenom II, GCC 4.7): LibFResample Q=5 Medium 1276x realtime vs libsamplerate Sinc Med. 35x and Sinc Fast 68x; Q=8 High 318x vs Sinc Best 8.5x; System D (1.7 GHz Core i5, Clang 4.0): Q=5 1247x vs Sinc Med. 39x. Mono Q=2 Low 3195x vs libsamplerate Linear 1112x (System D). Pairs closer in passband width: Q=8 High (19.5 kHz) vs Sinc Med. (90% bandwidth) 318x vs 35x on System C (about 9.1x, derived from page data) and 303x vs 39x on System D (about 7.8x, derived from page data); Q=10 Ultra (21.2 kHz) vs Sinc Best (97% bandwidth) 107x vs 8.5x on System C (about 12.6x, derived from page data) and 87x vs 11x on System D (about 7.9x, derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from 2005-2012 hardware and libsamplerate 0.1.8. The headline Q=5 Medium setting does less work than the libsamplerate converters it is paired with: by LibFResample's own quality table Q=5 keeps 16.3 kHz at 84 dB SNR, while libsamplerate documents 97 dB SNR at 90% bandwidth for Sinc Medium (about 19.8 kHz at 44.1 kHz output) and 80% (about 17.6 kHz) for Sinc Fast, and its MEDIUM filter table states 120.61 dB stop-band attenuation. Q=8 and Q=10 match libsamplerate's Medium and Best bandwidths more closely but measure 92 dB SNR (limited by the 16-bit dithered test floor), so stop-band parity is unproven. The two sides were timed by different harnesses: LibFResample on 16-bit pink noise (tests/benchmark.py, 20 iterations), libsamplerate by its own throughput test, which in the current libsamplerate source runs mono float data at ratio 0.99 through src_simple, so the stereo SRC rows are likely mono-test figures (not confirmed for 0.1.8). Optimization flags are not stated. The README says the library is not release quality (16-bit mono/stereo only, no error reporting). Baseline is not an FFmpeg component, so baseline_in_list is false. Last commit 2022-05-31.

notes: All quoted figures match the README table exactly. The main issue is quality pairing: Q=5 is narrower and noisier than Sinc Medium, so the 36x headline is not like-for-like; bandwidth-matched pairs still show about 8-13x (derived). Metadata (BSD-2-Clause, 59 stars, last commit 2022-05-31) confirmed.

tier_reason: Independent third-party measurement: the SampleRateTap author (a competitor, whose page states soxr beats his own library) benchmarks soxr 0.1.3 against libsamplerate 0.2.2 with public code async/bench/compare/bench_compare.cpp, GCC 13.3 -O3, median of 5; it falls short of A because the CPU is only 'shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz' and the distribution packages' build flags are not stated. This matches the current merged record's B (the rendered prompt carried the superseded python-soxr record at C).

corrections.baseline: libsamplerate 0.2.2 (Secret Rabbit Code, SRC_SINC_MEDIUM_QUALITY and SRC_SINC_BEST_QUALITY converters)
corrections.workload: Streaming sample-rate conversion of a float32 interleaved 997 Hz sine at a fixed near-unity ratio (48000 to 48009.6 Hz, 1 + 200 ppm) in 128-frame blocks under Google Benchmark, single thread (soxr's default runtime spec is 1 thread), reported as million output frames per second for mono, stereo and 8-channel streams at a ~120 dB tier (soxr HQ vs libsamplerate MEDIUM) and stereo at a ~140 dB tier (soxr VHQ vs libsamplerate BEST); run by the SampleRateTap author, who compares his own resampler against both.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Third-party table (Mframes/s, higher is better): stereo ~120 dB tier soxr HQ 52.9 vs libsamplerate MEDIUM 4.8 (about 11x, derived from page data); mono 114.3 vs 5.2 (about 22x, derived from page data); 8-ch 12.9 vs 1.9 (about 6.8x, derived from page data); ~140 dB stereo soxr VHQ 32.1 vs libsamplerate BEST 1.6 (about 20x, derived from page data). The page calls soxr the winner of raw host throughput.
corrections.caveats: The numbers come from a competitor's comparison page (SampleRateTap COMPARISON.md, run 2026-09-25 with async/bench/compare/bench_compare.cpp), not from the soxr project; libsoxr's own repo has throughput tests of soxr alone (tests/throughput.c) and no comparison with libsamplerate, and its SourceForge wiki has none either. CPU model is only 'shared Xeon @ 2.10 GHz'; soxr 0.1.3 and libsamplerate 0.2.2 are Ubuntu 24.04 packages with unstated build flags. The throughput workload is a near-unity ratio (1 + 200 ppm), not 44.1/48 kHz conversion. Quality pairing: soxr HQ (20-bit precision, about 120 dB rejection, passband to 91.3% of Nyquist per soxr.h) vs libsamplerate MEDIUM (filter table 120.61 dB stop band, 90% bandwidth per its docs) is a fair match; soxr VHQ (28-bit, about 170 dB, passband 91.3%) vs libsamplerate BEST (154.67 dB, 97% bandwidth) gives soxr more rejection but a narrower preserved band (about 21.9 kHz vs 23.3 kHz at 48 kHz, derived), both flat past 20 kHz; the page's AES17-style THD+N test puts soxr VHQ and libsamplerate sinc_best both at the format ceiling (-143.8 vs -143.5 dB, 24-bit I/O). Supporting evidence at a real conversion ratio: the python-soxr README (Google Colab, CPU unspecified, through Python bindings) times 10 s of 48 kHz to 44.1 kHz at 10.8 ms (soxr HQ) vs 223 ms (samplerate sinc_medium) and 14.5 ms (VHQ) vs 794 ms (sinc_best). soxr's speed comes with large latency (424-788 frames at HQ in this test), so it suits offline or batch work, not 1-2 ms live paths. The GitHub repo mirrors SourceForge; both end at 2018-02-24 (0.1.3); the maintained patched fork dofuuz/soxr (bundled by python-soxr) fixes integer-output dithering and enables NEON on AArch64, neither of which affects these float x86 numbers.

notes: All four Mframes/s pairs match COMPARISON.md and the derived ratios check out; the harness code confirms single-thread soxr, float I/O and the near-unity ratio. License in the record should read LGPL-2.1-or-later (LICENCE text says 'version 2.1 ... or (at your option) any later version'). No known correctness bug behind the measured float path.
